facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.

The aim of the demonstration was to protest against abuses and falsifications in the course of the elections to the State Duma and of the President of the Russian Federation, and to demand fair elections, respect for human rights, the rule of law and the international obligations of the Russian Federation.
On 27 April 2012 the organisers requested an alternative route from Kaluzhskaya Square, down Bolshaya Yakimanka Street and Bolshaya Polyanka Street, followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The march was to begin at 4 p.m. and the meeting was to finish by 7.30 p.m.
The number of participants for the alternative route proposal was indicated as 5,000.
The march began at 4.30 p.m. at Kaluzhskaya Square.
The march proceeded down Yakimanka Street peacefully and without disruption.
The turnout at the march exceeded expectations, but there is no consensus as to the exact numbers.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Bolotnaya Square at around 6 p.m. to take part in the meeting.
The applicant stood in front of the stage on Bolotnaya Embankment, within the area designated as the meeting venue.
According to the applicant, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. the area around him remained peaceful, although there was general confusion.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
The applicant was detained at the police station for at least thirty-six hours pending administrative proceedings.

In the administrative proceedings, the applicant was found guilty of failure to obey lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.

On 26 April 2012 the Head of the Moscow Department of Regional Security, Mr A. Mayorov, informed the organisers that the requested route could not be allocated because of preparations for the Victory Day parade on 9 May 2012.

On 3 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security approved the alternative route from Kaluzhskaya Square, down Bolshaya Yakimanka Street and Bolshaya Polyanka Street, followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.

On 4 May 2012 the deputy mayor of Moscow, Mr A. Gorbenko, ordered the Moscow Department of Regional Security to inform the organisers that their assembly notice had been accepted and to monitor its implementation.
On 5 May 2012 the Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Golovanov, adopted a plan for safeguarding public order in Moscow on 6 May 2012 (the security plan).

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.
The main contingent of the security plan was the police squad charged with cordon and riot-control duties in accordance with a structured and detailed action plan for each operational unit.

The security plan provided for a 785-strong police unit assigned to operational posts across the city centre, with responsibility for apprehending offenders, escorting them to police stations and drawing up administrative-offence reports.
The security plan provided for a 350-strong police unit for intercepting and apprehending organisers and instigators of unauthorised gatherings.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to obstruct access to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, diverting the marchers to Bolotnaya Embankment, the site of the meeting.
The adjacent park at Bolotnaya Square had to be cordoned off under the security plan.

The only entrance to Bolotnaya Embankment – from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge – had to be equipped with fourteen metal detectors, which were to be removed just before the march approached the site of the meeting.

The command of Zone no. 8, in particular Police Colonels Smirnov and Saprykin, were under orders to meet the organisers in person at the beginning of the event to remind them of their responsibilities and to have them sign an undertaking.
The police searched the vehicles delivering the equipment and seized three tents found amid the gear.
The police arrested several people for bringing the tents to Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.

A cordon of riot police in full protection gear barred access to the park at Bolotnaya Square and continued along the whole perimeter of the meeting area, channelling the demonstration to Bolotnaya Embankment.
Further down Bolotnaya Embankment there was a row of metal detectors at the entrance to the meeting venue.

Faced with the police cordon and unable to access the park, the leaders of the march – Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin – stopped and demanded that the police open access to the park.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.

During the period between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m., no senior police officers or municipal officials came to the site of the sit-down protest, and there was no direct communication between the authorities and the leaders of the sit-in.
At approximately 5.55 p.m. a commotion arose near the police cordon at the place vacated by the sit-down protest, and the police cordon was broken in several places.
Within seconds the police restored the cordon, which was reinforced by additional riot police.
Several people were apprehended, others were pushed back inside the cordon, and some continued to loiter outside or walked towards the park.
The police cordon began to push the crowd into the restricted area and advanced by several metres, pressing it inwards.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.

Ms N. Mityushkina made the announcement from the stage that the meeting was over, but apparently her message was not heard by most of the demonstrators or the media reporters broadcasting from the spot.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
At 6.21 p.m. several police officers arrested Mr S. Udaltsov and took him away from the stage.
Mr A. Navalnyy attempted to go up onto the stage, but he was also arrested at the stairs and taken away.
At Malyy Kamennyy Bridge the police continued dividing the crowd and began pushing some sections away from the venue.
Through the loudspeakers the police requested that the participants leave for the metro station.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.

In the administrative proceedings, the applicant was found guilty of failure to obey lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.

The Federal Law on assemblies, meetings, demonstrations, marches and pickets (no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004, the Public Events Act) required that notification of a public event be filed by its organiser in writing with the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of the officer's official duties relating to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the officer's performance of his or her official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage payable by the organisers, and breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of such events shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 1,000 and RUB 2,000 for the organisers and between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 for the participants.

Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that the organisation of mass disorder accompanied by violence, riots, arson, destruction of property, use of firearms, explosives and explosive devices, as well as by armed resistance to a public official, shall be punishable by four to ten years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that participation in mass disorder as provided for in Article 212 § 1 shall be punishable by three to eight years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 3 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that the instigation of mass disorder or the instigation of participation in it, or the instigation of violence against citizens, shall be punishable by restriction of liberty for up to two years, or community work for up to two years, or deprivation of liberty for the same term.

Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that the use of violence not endangering life or health, or the threat to use such violence, against a public official or his or her relatives in connection with the performance of his or her duties shall be punishable by a fine of up to 200,000 Russian roubles or the equivalent of the convicted person's wages for eighteen months, or community work for up to five years, or up to five years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of the officer's official duties relating to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the officer's performance of his or her official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

On 6 May 2012 the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation opened a criminal investigation into suspected offences of mass disorder and violent acts against the police under Article 212 § 2 and Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
On 28 May 2012 an investigation was launched into the criminal offence of organising mass disorder under Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that the mass disorder organised by Mr S. Udaltsov and others led to the destabilisation of public order and peace in a public place during the conduct of a public event, put a large number of people in danger, and led to considerable psychological tension in the vicinity of Bolotnaya Square in Moscow, accompanied by violence against the police and the destruction of property.

The Moscow Department of Regional Security proposed that the organisers hold the march between Luzhniki Street and Frunzenskaya Embankment.
On 27 April 2012 the organisers declined the proposal to hold the march between Luzhniki Street and Frunzenskaya Embankment.

On 3 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security approved the alternative route from Kaluzhskaya Square, down Bolshaya Yakimanka Street and Bolshaya Polyanka Street, followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers were warned that exceeding the number originally declared would be unacceptable.
On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow City Prosecutor's Office to issue a warning to the organisers against exceeding the notified number of participants.

On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow City Prosecutor's Office to issue a warning to the organisers against erecting camping tents at the meeting venue, an intention allegedly expressed by the organisers at the working meeting.

On 5 May 2012 the Tsentralnyy district prosecutor's office issued a warning to two of the organisers, Mr S. Davidis and Mr S. Udaltsov, against exceeding the notified number of participants and against erecting camping tents at the meeting venue.
On 5 May 2012 the Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Golovanov, adopted a plan for safeguarding public order in Moscow on 6 May 2012 (the security plan).
The security plan was a ninety-nine-page internal document which had not been disclosed to the public or to the organisers.
The security plan set up operational headquarters to implement the security measures.
Thirty-two high-ranking police officers, including eight major-generals, two military commanders and one emergency-relief official, were appointed to the operational headquarters.
The Deputy Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Kozlov, was appointed as head of the operational headquarters.
The Chief of the Special-Purpose Operational Centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Khaustov, was appointed as deputy head of the operational headquarters.
The Deputy Chief of the Public Order Directorate of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Colonel D. Deynichenko, was appointed as deputy head of the operational headquarters.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.
The main contingent of the security plan was the police squad charged with cordon and riot-control duties in accordance with a structured and detailed action plan for each operational unit.

The security plan provided for a 785-strong police unit assigned to operational posts across the city centre, with responsibility for apprehending offenders, escorting them to police stations and drawing up administrative-offence reports.
The 785-strong police unit was instructed to prepare templates for the administrative-offence reports and to have at least forty printed copies of them at every police station.
The security plan provided for a 350-strong police unit for intercepting and apprehending organisers and instigators of unauthorised gatherings.
The 350-strong police unit had to be equipped with full protection gear and police batons.
Each unit in the security plan had to ensure effective radio communication within the chain of command.
Units were instructed to keep loudspeakers, metal detectors, handcuffs, fire extinguishers and wire clippers in the police vehicles.

The security plan set out in detail the allocation and deployment of police vehicles, police buses, interception and monitoring vehicles and equipment, dog-handling teams, fire-fighting and rescue equipment, ambulances and a helicopter.

The security plan made provision for a 1,815-strong reserve unit equipped with gas masks, aerosol grenades (Дрейф), flash grenades (Заря-2), bang grenades (Факел and Факел-C), a 40-mm hand-held grenade launcher (Гвоздь 6Г-30), and a 43-mm hand-held grenade launcher (ГМ-94).
The 1,815-strong reserve unit was also equipped with tubeless pistols (ПБ-4СП) with 23-mm rubber bullets and propelling cartridges, and rifles (KC-23).
Two water-cannon vehicles were ordered to be on standby, ready to be used against persistent offenders.

All units were instructed to be vigilant and thorough in detecting and eliminating security threats and to be polite and tactful in their conduct vis-à-vis citizens, engaging in lawful dialogue with them without responding to provocations.
If faced with an unauthorised gathering, units were instructed to give a warning through a loudspeaker, to arrest the most active participants and to record video-footage of those incidents.

Police chiefs were instructed to place plain-clothes officers among the protesters in order to monitor the threat of violence and terrorist attacks within the crowd and to take measures, where appropriate, to prevent and mitigate the damage and to pursue the perpetrators.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to obstruct access to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, diverting the marchers to Bolotnaya Embankment, the site of the meeting.

The command of Zone no. 8, in particular Police Colonels Smirnov and Saprykin, were under orders to meet the organisers in person at the beginning of the event to remind them of their responsibilities and to have them sign an undertaking.

Police Colonel A. Makhonin specifically asked Mr S. Udaltsov to ensure that no tents were placed on Bolotnaya Square and that the participants complied with the limits on the place and time allocated for the assembly.

According to the protesters, they were taken aback by the alteration of the expected layout and demanded that the police officers at the cordon move the cordon back to allow sufficient space for the protesters to pass and to assemble for the meeting.

According to the official version, the protesters were not interested in proceeding to the meeting venue; they stopped because they had either intended to break the cordon in order to proceed towards Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge and then to the Kremlin, or to stir up the crowd to incite disorder.

After around fifteen minutes of attempting to engage with the cordon officers, at 5.16 p.m. the four leaders (Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin) announced that they were going on a 'sit-down strike' and sat on the ground.
At 5.40 p.m. one of the meeting participants announced from the stage that the leaders were calling on the demonstrators to support their protest.
At 5.55 p.m. the media reported that the police authorities were regarding the sit-down strike as a provocation of mass disorder and were considering prosecuting those responsible for it.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.

Ms N. Mityushkina made the announcement from the stage that the meeting was over, but apparently her message was not heard by most of the demonstrators or the media reporters broadcasting from the spot.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
Through the loudspeakers the police requested that the participants leave for the metro station.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 5.58 p.m. to 7 p.m. persons on Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and Bolotnaya Embankment made attempts to break the cordon, and threw empty glass bottles, fireworks, chunks of tarmac and portable metal barriers at the police officers.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. necessary measures were taken to push citizens away from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, Bolotnaya Embankment and Bolotnaya Street and to arrest those who resisted the most, during which twenty-eight police officers and military servicemen sustained injuries of various gravity, four of whom were hospitalised.
According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, in total 656 people were detained in Moscow to prevent public disorder and unauthorised demonstrations.

The security plan and security maps were prepared at extremely short notice (during the night of 4-5 May 2012 and the day of 5 May 2012) and were approved on 5 May 2012 by senior officials at the Moscow Department of the Interior.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that on the evening of 5 May 2012 the police cordoned off the public gardens at Bolotnaya Square, according to Police Colonel Y. Zdorenko, in order to prevent the participants from setting up camp and from other illegal acts.

The Expert Commission noted that the authorities received information that the protesters might attempt to establish a protest camp at the site, causing them to decide that the rally should be confined to only the Bolotnaya waterfront area – a much smaller area than had been originally allocated for the assembly.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.

The Expert Commission's report stated that as the march approached Bolotnaya Square, demonstrators found that a police cordon was blocking off most of the square, leaving only a narrow stretch along the waterfront for the rally.
The Expert Commission's report stated that the police established a triple cordon of officers on Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, which prevented any movement in the direction of the Kremlin.

The Expert Commission's report stated that behind the first cordon were two rows of OMON riot police, a line of voluntary citizen patrol ('druzhinniki'), and another cordon of OMON, with a number of water cannons visible between the second and third cordons.

The Expert Commission's report contained two photographs comparing the police cordon on 4 February 2012 (a thin line of police officers without protection gear) and the one on 6 May 2012 (multiple ranks of riot police with full protection gear backed up by heavy vehicles).

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 5.42 p.m. the chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior issued a statement characterising the organisers' refusal to proceed to the agreed place of the rally as creating a real threat of a jam and trauma for participants, and announcing that an inquiry commission was working on the spot to document actions related to appeals to commit mass public disorder.

The Expert Commission's report stated that some demonstrators tried to pass through the police cordon to leave the area, but the police refused to let them through and directed them to go back through the crowd to Bolshaya Polyanka Street, even though this was practically impossible.

The Expert Commission's report stated that from the moment difficulties first arose for demonstrators attempting to cross Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, demonstrators made repeated attempts to negotiate with the police over moving their cordons to allow protesters onto Bolotnaya Square.

The Expert Commission's report stated that Mr D. Oreshkin, a member of the Presidential Human Rights Council, and State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov tried to talk to the police authorities at around 5.30 p.m., but there was no response.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Ms N. Mityushkina as stating that she tried unsuccessfully to find the responsible people in the Ministry of the Interior to solve organisational problems, and that only at 6.00-6.30 p.m. did a senior police officer approach her and tell her that the authorities had suspended the demonstration and ask her to announce from the stage that the event was over.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr S. Davidis as stating that he personally did not meet nor have time to get into contact with the authorities regarding the fences set up around the perimeter of the rally, and that he only saw OMON officers who behaved aggressively and were not predisposed to get into a conversation.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 5.55 p.m. as people tried to move through the narrow gap between the police cordon and the waterfront, the police line moved two steps forward, further pressing the crowd, which generated a counter response from the crowd, and in several places the police cordon broke.

The Expert Commission's report stated that in the two hours between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. there does not appear to have been any clear reason for the police decision to advance other than to divide the crowd up into smaller sections, and that there is little evidence that demonstrators initiated the violence.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 6.20 p.m. the police announced that the rally was cancelled and asked protesters to disperse, but the announcement was not loud enough to reach the majority of the crowd.
The Expert Commission's report stated that by 6.30 p.m. the crowd at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and the waterfront was cut in two.

The Expert Commission's report stated that approximately 15 minutes after 6.54 p.m., some 200 police officers in protective equipment began pushing protesters in the direction of Lavrushinsky Lane and back along the Bolotnaya waterfront from Luzhkov Bridge towards the Udarnik cinema.

The Expert Commission's report stated that between 9.00 and 10.00 p.m. around two thousand demonstrators moved along Bolshaya Ordynka Street chanting slogans and OMON officers began to detain people and actively disperse the column.

On 20 March 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy branch of the Investigative Committee dismissed ten individual complaints and two official enquiries made in relation to the allegedly unlawful acts of the police in dispersing the rally on 6 May 2012, including excessive use of force and arbitrary arrests.

The police officers stated that they had been acting under orders to maintain public safety and to identify and arrest the most active instigators of unrest, and that only those resisting the demands of the police had been arrested and no force had been used unnecessarily.
The police officers stated that when the police had had to intervene, they had used combat manoeuvres and truncheons but not tear gas or other exceptional means of restraint.

The Investigative Committee found on 20 March 2013 that after the organisers had decided to call a sit-down protest they provoked mass disorder, during which the participants threw various objects at the police, causing injuries to some of them, and that the police officers detained those participating in the mass disorder with justifiable use of force.
The Investigative Committee refused on 20 March 2013 to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers for the absence of corpus delicti.

The Investigative Committee found on 22 May 2014 that in suppressing attempts to break the police cordon, the police officers acted in coordination and concert, without applying physical force or special means of restraint, except that the work of the officers charged with apprehending offenders did involve physical force and special means of restraint in so far as necessary against those resisting.

The Investigative Committee found on 22 May 2014 that the police officers justifiably used physical force to apprehend the participants in the mass disorder, and also special means of restraint in relation to some of them who attempted to resist.

The witness Mr D. Deynichenko testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that on 4 May 2012 he had taken part in a working meeting at the Moscow Department of Regional Security, and that all necessary agreements were reached with the organisers concerning the order of the march and meeting, the movement of the procession, the stage set-up, access to the meeting venue, barriers and the exit from the stage.

The witness Mr A. Makhonin testified that on 5 May 2012 he received the security plan, and that before the start of the march he personally met the event organisers Mr S. Udaltsov, Ms N. Mityushkina and Mr S. Davidis and explained to them the order of the meeting and the march, warned against the breach of public order, and asked Mr S. Udaltsov regarding the intention to proceed towards the Kremlin and to cause mass disorder.
The witness Mr A. Makhonin testified that Mr S. Udaltsov had assured him that there would be no breaches of order at the event and that they had no intention to approach the Kremlin.

The witness Ms N. Mirza testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that Police Colonel V. Biryukov had asked her and the Ombudsman to come to Malyy Kamennyy Bridge where some of the protesters, including Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr S. Udaltsov, had not turned right towards the stage but had gone straight to the cordon, where they had begun a sit-in protest on the pretext that access to the park of Bolotnaya Square had been closed and cordoned off.

The witness Mr A. Babushkin testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that after the first confrontations between the protesters and the police had begun, the police announced through a loudspeaker that the meeting was cancelled and invited citizens to leave.

The witness Mr I. Ponomarev testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that the police cordon had been placed differently from the cordon placed for the similar march on 4 February 2012, and that he proposed to Mr S. Udaltsov that the cordon be pushed back so that the police would go back a few steps and widen access to Bolotnaya Square.

The witnesses Mr I. Yashin and Mr B. Nemtsov testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that during the steering committee meeting the question of setting up tents during the public event had not been discussed, and that while Mr G. Gudkov and Mr D. Gudkov were negotiating with the police the crowd built up and suddenly the police began moving forward, the protesters resisted and the cordon broke.

The witness Mr G. Gudkov, deputy of the State Duma, testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that at the request of the organisers he had taken part in the negotiations with the police on moving the cordon back and opening up access to the park at Bolotnaya Square, and that he had reached an agreement with the officers of the Moscow Department of the Interior that the cordon would be moved back, but those who had called for a sit-in, including Mr S. Udaltsov, refused to go to the offices of the Moscow Department of the Interior to sign the necessary documents.

The witness Mr D. Gudkov, deputy of the State Duma, testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that together with Mr G. Gudkov he had conducted negotiations with the police and an agreement had been reached that the cordon at Malyy Kamennyy Bridge would be moved back and access to the park would be opened up, but at that point some young men in hoodies among the protesters began pushing citizens onto the cordon, after which the cordon broke, the police began the arrests and mass disorder ensued.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev rejected testimonies to the effect that it was the police who had begun moving towards the protesters who were peacefully sitting on the ground and thus provoked the breaking of the cordon, and found that it was the protesters who began pushing against the cordon, causing the crowd to panic, which eventually led to the breaking of the cordon and the ensuing mass disorder.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if a standoff or other dispute arises during the course of an assembly, negotiation or mediated dialogue may be an appropriate means of trying to reach an acceptable resolution.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement officials should differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants, and that neither isolated incidents of sporadic violence nor the violent acts of some participants are themselves sufficient grounds to impose sweeping restrictions on peaceful participants in an assembly.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that so long as assemblies remain peaceful, they should not be dispersed by law enforcement officials, and that dispersal of assemblies should be a measure of last resort.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that dispersal should not occur unless law enforcement officials have taken all reasonable measures to facilitate and protect the assembly from harm and unless there is an imminent threat of violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and participants should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily before law enforcement officials intervene further.

The Expert Commission's report stated that the police used loudspeakers to inform demonstrators of the rally location and asked participants to pass directly to Bolotnaya Square, but given the poor quality of the sound equipment, only those nearest the police could hear this information.

Mr Vasilyev testified that on 6 May 2012 he was present as an observer and that on that day they gathered at the press centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior, were given maps, instructions on how to behave, and the list of public observers.
